growth_story.headline: Antigua and Barbuda's income per person has climbed back since 2016 on tourism and building, yet in 2025 it was still below its 2007 peak.
growth_story.arc: In the 1990s income per person grew 1.9 percent a year, and the sources opened say little about that decade. From 2000 to 2007 growth rose to 4.0 percent a year, with 11.3 percent in 2006, as a building boom in hotels and housing and work for the 2007 Cricket World Cup drove the fastest growth in decades. From 2008 to 2015 income per person shrank 3.0 percent a year: the global crisis hit the visitors the island depends on, the Stanford business group collapsed, and a looming debt crisis led the government to an IMF program in 2010. Since 2016 growth has averaged 2.1 percent a year, led by tourism and construction, though the pandemic cut income per person by 19.3 percent in 2020 before rebounds of 7.6 and 7.9 percent in 2021 and 2022. Even so, income per person in 2025 was 7.9 percent below its 2007 peak and about where it first was in 2006.

threads.title: Tourism sets the pace
threads.text: Tourism is the island's main business, so growth rises and falls with visitor numbers. Tourism drove the recovery that took output past its pre-pandemic level in 2024. When tourism slowed in 2025, construction carried growth.

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: Staff Report for the 2012 Article IV Consultation
citations.quote: Tourism drives 60–70 percent of economic activity in Antigua and Barbuda, and its slowdown has hit the economy hard.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation with Antigua and Barbuda
citations.quote: Real output in 2024 is estimated to have surpassed pre-pandemic levels, with growth estimated at 4.3 percent, driven by strong tourism and one-off events

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Antigua and Barbuda
citations.quote: Real GDP grew by an estimated 3 percent in 2025, supported by a pick-up in construction despite slowing tourism activity

threads.title: Building boom before 2008
threads.text: A building boom in hotels and housing, and work for the 2007 Cricket World Cup, lifted growth in income per person to 11.3 percent in 2006. The IMF expected growth to cool as the boom wound down, and in 2007 it slowed to 7.8 percent.

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: 2006 Article IV Consultation—Staff Report; Staff Statement; Public Information Notice on the Executive Board Discussion; and Statement by the Authorities of Antigua and Barbuda
citations.quote: Antigua and Barbuda is experiencing its fastest growth in decades, led by private investment and preparations for the 2007 Cricket World Cup.

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: 2006 Article IV Consultation—Staff Report; Staff Statement; Public Information Notice on the Executive Board Discussion; and Statement by the Authorities of Antigua and Barbuda
citations.quote: driven by a construction boom in hotels and housing, as well as projects related to the 2007 Cricket World Cup

citations.quote: GDP growth will likely cool in 2007−08 as the construction boom winds down

threads.title: Crisis hits tourism hard
threads.text: The global crisis hit the American and British visitors the island relies on, and the collapse of the Stanford business group may have deepened the blow. The IMF judged that most of the fall in output from 2009 to 2011 came from tourism. Income per person fell 13.3 percent in 2009 and 9.1 percent in 2010.

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: Staff Report for the 2012 Article IV Consultation
citations.quote: the two largest tourism source markets (the US and the UK) were severely impacted by the global crisis

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: Staff Report for the 2012 Article IV Consultation
citations.quote: the collapse of the Stanford business group may have contributed to the severity of the tourism shock faced by the island

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: Staff Report for the 2012 Article IV Consultation
citations.quote: about three-quarters of the economic contraction in Antigua and Barbuda from 2009–11 is estimated to have come from the slowdown of tourism related subsectors

threads.title: Debt crisis and repair
threads.text: Large deficits and fast-rising debt before the global crisis led the government to an IMF program in 2010. Public debt has fallen a long way since 2020.

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: Staff Report for the 2012 Article IV Consultation
citations.quote: The program was requested in response to a looming fiscal crisis precipitated by large fiscal deficits and a rapid increase in debt

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Antigua and Barbuda
citations.quote: Public debt as a share of GDP declined from 101 percent of GDP in 2020 to an estimated 68 percent in 2025.

threads.title: Citizenship sales and building
threads.text: Money from selling citizenship helped the public finances in 2025. That year building work picked up and drew in more imports while tourist arrivals flattened. The IMF notes that these citizenship inflows face risk after recent US travel policy announcements.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Antigua and Barbuda
citations.quote: stronger inflows under the Citizenship-by-Investment Program (CIP)

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: increased construction-related imports and flattening tourist arrivals

citations.title: Antigua and Barbuda: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: CIP-related inflows subject to downside risks after recent U.S. travel policy announcements

since_last_year.text: In May 2026 the IMF reported that construction picked up in 2025 while tourism slowed. In February 2026 it flagged that money from selling citizenship faces risk after US travel policy announcements. In the data, income per person grew 4.5 percent in 2025.

growth_story.tension: The IMF says total output passed its pre-pandemic level in 2024, but in the data income per person stayed below its 2019 level until 2025. For 2025 the data show income per person growing 4.5 percent, faster than the IMF's May 2026 estimate for growth of the whole economy.
